It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}} ({{jalink|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964}}). Under the {{jalink|modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|former shrine ranking}}, it was classified as a {{jalink|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|Kanpei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} of the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. It claims to be the head shrine of all {{jalink|Watatsumi shrines|Q11607434}} and {{jalink|Kaijin shrines|Q123530063}} nationwide. It is praised as the “capital of dragons” and is known as a place associated with the ancient clan {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}} (also written Adzumi). === Shrine name === Regarding the origin of the word “Shika” (志賀), which is also the island name of {{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}, an excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* Excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* cited in *Shaku Nihongi*, vol. 6, section on the deities worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji, etc. says that, based on a tradition connected to {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s expedition to {{jalink|Silla|Q28456}}, the area was called “Chikashima (近島, ‘near island’),” which later shifted in pronunciation to “Shikashima (資珂島)” . The shrine name “Shikaumi” (志賀海) is now pronounced “Shikaumi,” but as for the original pronunciation there are various theories such as “Shika no Wata,” “Shika no Ama,” “Shika no Umi,” and “Shika ni Imasu Wata,” among others . === Enshrined deities === The deities are enshrined as follows: one principal deity in each of the left, center, and right halls, along with one associated deity in each hall . The three principal deities are collectively called the “{{jalink|Watatsumi|Q1474187|Watatsumi Three Deities}}” (綿津見三神, watatsumi sanshin) . * Left Hall: **Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (仲津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Left Hall: {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}} (神功皇后) * Center Hall: **Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami** (底津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Center Hall: {{jalink|Tamayorihime (Hyūga myth)|Q3082751|Princess Tamayorihime}} (玉依姫命) * Right Hall: **Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (表津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Right Hall: {{jalink|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997}} (応神天皇) === About the enshrined deities === The three Watatsumi (sea / Watatsumi / Watatsumi of the “少童” reading) deities are regarded as sea gods, as seen in the ancient name for the sea “Wata / Watanohara” (“sea = wata, watanohara”) “Kaijin Shinkō” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.. In the “birth of the gods” section of the {{jalink|Kojiki|Q813031}} and {{jalink|Nihon Shoki|Q813935}}, during the purification rite ({{jalink|misogi}}), they are described as gods born together with the {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}} as follows. * *Kojiki* *: It calls the three born deities—Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami, Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami, and Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami—collectively “Watatsumi no Kami,” and states, “They are the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji (あずみのむらじ) and others venerate as their ancestral deity” . * *Nihon Shoki* *: After saying, “The sea gods born were named Sukunahiko no Mikoto,” it records that the three born deities—Sokotsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, Nakatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, and Uwatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto—are “the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji and others worship” . Thus, in the *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*, the Watatsumi Three Deities are treated as the ancestral gods or worshiped gods of the **{{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}}** (Azumi-uji/Azumi-uji; also written 安曇氏, 阿曇族, 安曇族) . The reading “Azumi/Azumi” is also seen as an abbreviation of “Amatsumi (海津見),” and the Azumi clan who served these deities were a *tomonomiyatsuko* clan that oversaw groups of seafaring people “Watatsumi no Kami” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.. In the {{jalink|Sendai Kujihongi|Q2716751}} *Sendai Kujihongi*, “Onmyō Hongi” (see [{{NDLDC|991097/110}} *Kokushi Taikei*, vol. 7] (Keizai Zasshisha, 1897–1901; National Diet Library Digital Collection), frame 110)., likewise in the section on the birth of the gods, it says: “The three Sukunahiko deities are worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji and others; they are the Tsukushi Shika gods,” and Shikaumi Shrine is named as a clan deity under the title “Tsukushi Shika no Kami (筑紫斯香神)” . As other major sea gods besides Watatsumi, Sumiyoshi ({{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}}; worshiped by the Sumiyoshi clan) and Munakata ({{jalink|Munakata Three Goddesses|Q10948069}}; worshiped by the {{jalink|Munakata clan|Q16481907|Munakata lineage}}) are well known, and in northern Kyūshū there are shrines dedicated to each: {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka City)|Q29682|Sumiyoshi Shrine}} and {{jalink|Munakata Taisha|Q704962}}. === History === [[File:Shikanoshima Island, enkei.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}, where Shikaumi Shrine is located}}]] === Founding === The founding date is unknown . According to shrine tradition, in ancient times it consisted of three shrines on Katsuma Beach on the north side of {{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}: Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū; but {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974}} (Azumi no Isora: ancestor of the {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}}) relocated the Uwatsu-gū to the south side of Shikanoshima, making it the present precinct . Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines . Azumi no Isora is also said to have served as helmsman in {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s expedition to {{jalink|Silla|Q28456}} . In ancient northern Kyūshū, the {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}} (also written 安曇氏), who governed sea people ({{jalink|ama|Q1577970}}), are said to have controlled maritime routes . Shikanoshima was a key point for sea traffic, and the area including Shikanoshima and {{jalink|Umi no Nakamichi|Q2404998}} Considered the area of Shika-gō and Azumi-gō in Kasuya District of Chikuzen Province as seen in the *Wamyōshō* (from the *Dictionary of Personal Names of Ancient Japanese Clans*, entry on the Azumi clan). Shika-gō is identified with Shikanoshima; Azumi-gō is identified with the area from Kamiwajiro and Shimowajiro in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City to Shingū Town in Kasuya District, or with Shikanoshima (from *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entries on Shika-gō and Azumi-gō). is said to have been the Azumi clan’s home base *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine., and Shikaumi Shrine is thought to have been the clan’s central shrine . Even today, all of Shikanoshima is regarded as a sacred precinct *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikanoshima., and the current priestly family also claims descent from the Azumi clan . The Azumi clan is said to have expanded throughout Japan, and place names such as “Shika” and “Atsumi”—for example {{jalink|Azumino City|Q534667}} in {{jalink|Nagano Prefecture|Q127877}}, {{jalink|Shika Town|Q1349406}} in {{jalink|Hakuigun|Q1130953}} of {{jalink|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281}}, the {{jalink|Adogawa|Q11450763}} in {{jalink|Shiga Prefecture|Q131358}}, and the {{jalink|Atsumi Peninsula|Q757798}} in {{jalink|Aichi Prefecture|Q80434}}—are said to be toponymic traces of their presence . Shikanoshima is also known for the discovery of the gold seal ({{jalink|King of Na of Wa gold seal|Q2975212}}), but it is unclear why the seal of {{jalink|Na|Q600473}} was found there. Some theories speculate a connection between the Azumi clan—and by extension Shikaumi Shrine as their clan deity—and Na, and at Najima Shrine in Najima, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, the Azumi clan is regarded as the “Nake-nushi” {{Cite web|和書|url=https://lunabura.exblog.jp/14132415/|title=Najima Shrine|accessdate=April 13, 2010|publisher=Ayasugi Luna}}. === Overview history === In surviving records, there is mention in the “Sumiyoshi Taisha Shige (Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki)”—dated Tenpyō 3 ({{jalink|731|Q23566}}), though likely compiled around the early {{jalink|Heian period|Q193292}}—of “Naka District Azumi Shrine, three offerings” and “Shika Shrine” . Also, in the {{jalink|Shinshō Kakuchokufushō|Q11502312}} *Shinshō Kakuchokufushō* 10, “Shinji Shoke Fuko,” directive of Daidō 1 (806) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}})., it appears that as of {{jalink|Daidō (era)|Q1373191|Daidō}} 1 ({{jalink|806|Q30021}}), “Azumi no Kami” had eight households as *shinpu* (donated *fuko*) . According to national histories, in {{jalink|Ten’an|Q1075611|Ten’an}} 3 ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}) the divine rank (*shinkai*) of “Shikaumi no Kami” was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, and in {{jalink|Gangyō|Q747451}} 4 ({{jalink|880|Q23618}}) “Katsuma no Kami” (identified with Nakatsu-gū) was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade . In the “Register of Deities” (*Jinmyōchō*) of the {{jalink|Engishiki|Q1342448}} compiled in {{jalink|Enchō|Q1327274|Enchō}} 5 ({{jalink|927|Q30470}}), it is listed under Naka District of {{jalink|Chikuzen Province|Q1047664}} as “Shikaumi Shrine, three seats, all Myōjin Taisha,” and is ranked as a {{jalink|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964}} . Other Heian and Kamakura-period sources concerning Shikaumi Shrine are few ; in the {{jalink|Shōyūki|Q11459316}} *Shōyūki*, entries for August 27 and August 30, Manju 4 (1027)., there is a note that in {{jalink|Manju|Q1194155}} 3 ({{jalink|1026|Q19269}}) the shrine’s priest traveled to {{jalink|Song dynasty|Q7462}} (entered Song) and returned the following year . [[File:Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba e20(2).JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Torii and shrine buildings depicted in the {{jalink|Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba|Q3087790}}}}]] In the {{jalink|Kamakura period|Q236205}}, during the {{jalink|Mongol invasions of Japan|Q208156}}, Shikanoshima became a battlefield, but Shikaumi Shrine’s precinct is recorded in the *Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba* under the name “Shikanoshima Daimyōjin” . From the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012}} onward, Shikaumi Shrine came strongly under warrior control . In {{jalink|Ōnin|Q1143903}} 3 ({{jalink|1469|Q6566}}), Shōni Yoritada confirmed the office of Shikanoshima’s chief priest for the abbot of Tōgetsuji on Tsushima , and afterward it received patronage from the {{jalink|Ōuchi clan|Q1348909}} . It is also said that before sailing to {{jalink|Ming|Q9903}}, people prayed here for safe voyages . In the early modern era, it received protection from the {{jalink|Kobayakawa clan|Q2975298}} and {{jalink|Kuroda clan|Q2975305}} who ruled Chikuzen Province . It is said that {{jalink|Kuroda Nagamasa|Q950496}}, who entered the province in {{jalink|Keichō|Q1328185}} 5 ({{jalink|1600|Q6720}}), built the main sanctuary, worship hall, rōmon gate, and other structures . In {{jalink|Bunka era|Q1373146|Bunka}} 14 ({{jalink|1817|Q6958}}), the shrine lands amounted to 50 koku . In {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 5 ({{jalink|1872|Q7753}}), under the modern shrine ranking system, it was designated a village shrine, and in {{jalink|Taishō|Q329174}} 15 ({{jalink|1926|Q5259}}) it was promoted to *Kanpei Shōsha* “Shikaumi Shrine” entry, *Nihon no Kamigami*.. === Divine ranks === * {{jalink|Ten’an|Q1075611|Ten’an}} 3 ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}) January 27: Shikaumi no Kami from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for January 27, Jōgan 1 (859) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}}). * {{jalink|Gangyō|Q747451}} 4 ({{jalink|880|Q23618}}) March 22: Katsuma no Kami from Senior Sixth Rank, Upper Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for March 22, Gangyō 4 (880). — From the divine name “Katsuma (賀津万),” identified with the subordinate shrine Nakatsu-gū (Katsuma Myōjin) *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine.. === Precincts === [[File:Shikaumi-jinja shaden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Worship hall (front) and main sanctuary (rear right)}}]] The precinct is located on the south side of Shikanoshima. It is said that Shikaumi Shrine was formerly on the north side of Shikanoshima and consisted of three shrines—Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū . Of these, Uwatsu-gū was transferred here and became the present main shrine, while Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines. The former site of Uwatsu-gū is said to be in Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|13.00|N|130|17|32.74|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Site of Uwatsu-gū (former location)}}). In the precinct’s Rokkakudō (鹿角堂), many deer antlers—said to number over ten thousand—have been dedicated. There is also a sacred stone dedicated in later times called the “Kameishi (亀石, ‘turtle stone’),” linked to a tradition that during {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s {{jalink|Three Kingdoms expedition|Q11249435}}, {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974}} appeared before the empress riding a turtle . Along the approach stands a stone *Hōkyōintō* pagoda. A {{jalink|Hōkyōintō|Q3146365}} is a pagoda that enshrines a Buddhist scripture (the *Hōkyōin Dharani Sutra*) Explanatory signboard in the precinct.. This one bears an inscription from {{jalink|Jōwa|Q1146143|Jōwa}} 3 ({{jalink|1347|Q6082}}) in the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012}}, and is the oldest complete example in Fukuoka Prefecture . Made of {{jalink|granite|Q41177}}, it consists of a base, body, roof, and finial, with a total height of 334.5 cm . It is designated a tangible cultural property of Fukuoka Prefecture . The first torii was built in {{jalink|Kanbun|Q1146228}} 10 ({{jalink|1670|Q7606}}) by {{jalink|Kuroda Mitsuyuki|Q11678571}}, the third lord of the {{jalink|Fukuoka Domain|Q208766}} . The next torii was built in {{jalink|Genroku|Q1325001}} 13 ({{jalink|1700|Q6813}}), and the torii by the seashore was built in An’ei 3 ({{jalink|1774|Q7697}}) . File:Rokkakudō.JPG|Rokkakudō (Deer Antler Hall) File:Shikaumi-jinja kameishi.JPG|Kameishi (Turtle Stone) File:Shikaumi-jinja romon.JPG|Rōmon gate and stone bridge File:Shikaumi-jinja tou.JPG|Hōkyōintō pagoda (Fukuoka Prefecture-designated tangible cultural property) File:Shikaumi-jinja ninotorii.JPG|Second torii === Auxiliary shrines (sessha and massha) === There are a total of 24 auxiliary shrines: 5 sessha and 19 massha Shrine origin pamphlet. . According to the *Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki*, there were once 375 massha, but they were damaged in the Warring States turmoil; at the time of restoration by {{jalink|Ōuchi Mochiyo|Q11432525}} in {{jalink|Eikyō|Q1193059}} 11 ({{jalink|1439|Q6380}}), there were a little over 120, and later in the Edo period there were only about five . === Sessha === [[File:Okitsujima Island near Shikanoshima Island 5.jpg|thumb|200px|{{center|{{jalink|Okitsushima|Q49665728}}, where Okitsu-gū is enshrined}}]] [[File:Torii of Katsuma Shrine (Nakatsu Shrine of Shikaumi Shrine).jpg|thumb|200px|{{center|Torii of Nakatsu-gū}}]] [[File:Shikaumi-jinja Imamiya-jinja.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Imamiya Shrine}}]] * Okitsu-gū (沖津宮) ** Location: Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|20.12|N|130|17|25.07|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Okitsu-gū}}) ** Enshrined deities: Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami, {{jalink|Ame no Minakanushi|Q2842779|Ame no Minakanushi no Kami}} * Nakatsu-gū (仲津宮 / 中津宮) ** Location: Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|11.80|N|130|17|27.45|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Nakatsu-gū}}) ** Enshrined deity: Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami *: Also called “Katsuma Myōjin,” and identified with “Katsuma no Kami” in the {{jalink|Kokushi genzaisha|Q118304363}} . *: In {{jalink|Heisei|Q234510}} 6 ({{jalink|1994|Q2067}}), a kofun (Nakatsu-gū Kofun) was discovered in the forecourt area [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/481 Nakatsu-gū Kofun] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. Because it was damaged by shrine construction, its size and form are unclear, but grave goods were found along with a pit-type stone chamber . It is dated to the first half of the {{jalink|7th century|Q8089}} and is regarded as the tomb of a leader of the local maritime group . * Imamiya Shrine (今宮神社) ** Location: within the main shrine precinct ({{Coord|33|40|4.89|N|130|18|46.38|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Imamiya Shrine}}) ** Enshrined deities: {{jalink|Utsushi Hikane no Mikoto|Q86736058}}, {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}}, {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974|Azumi no Isora-maru}}, and other ancestral Azumi deities * Hiroten Shrine (弘天神社) ** Location: Hiro, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|40|15.19|N|130|17|34.32|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Hiroten Shrine}}) ** Enshrined deities: {{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi no Mikoto}}, {{jalink|Izanami|Q682306|Izanami no Mikoto}} * Ōtake Shrine (大嶽神社) ** Location: Ōtake, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|39|23.19|N|130|20|8.05|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Ōtake Shrine}}) ** Enshrined deities: {{jalink|Shinatsuhiko|Q1073925|Shinatsuhiko no Kami}}, Shinatsuhime no Kami, Ōhama Sukune, {{jalink|Uke-mochi|Q2280323}} === Massha === There are 19 massha in total: 12 in Shika, 5 in Katsuma, 1 in Hiro, and 1 in Ōtake . File:Shikaumi-jinja massha.JPG|Group of massha within the precinct File:Shikaumi-jinja Innyaku-sha.JPG|Innyaku Shrine === Festivals === === Annual grand festival === Shikaumi Shrine’s annual grand festival is called the “Kunchi Festival” (国土祭). On the previous day, every other year (odd-numbered years in the Western calendar), the shrine’s largest festival, the “Goshinkō Festival” (御神幸祭), is held . In the past it was held on the old lunar calendar: September 8 (Goshinkō Festival) and September 9 (Kunchi Festival), but today it is held on {{jalink|Health and Sports Day}} and the day before (the second Monday of October and the preceding day) . Before the festival, on lunar September 1 (October 1), a “Otokoyama Festival” is held in which a {{jalink|lottery|Q5433694}} determines whether to conduct the procession (today it is held biennially) . In the Goshinkō Festival, beginning at 9 p.m. on the night of lunar September 8 (the night before Health and Sports Day), three mikoshi (Ichinoto, Ninoto, Sannotō) depart and proceed to a temporary shrine (tonomiya) . There, performances based on the shrine’s origin traditions—such as the “Dragon Dance,” “Yaotome Dance,” and “Kakko Dance”—are dedicated . The mikoshi then return to the shrine, the spirit is transferred back to the main sanctuary, and the Goshinkō Festival ends . On the following day, lunar September 9 (Health and Sports Day), *yabusame* ({{jalink|horseback archery|Q1886157}}) is offered . Because it involves moving the divine spirit at night and aims to reaffirm the tradition for the people through performances rooted in the shrine’s origin narrative, the Goshinkō Festival is said to preserve an ancient form . The rites are designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event” . === Special rites === ; Hosha Festival : “Hosha-sai.” A New Year rite held among annual events from January 2 to 15, conducted on a Sunday near January 15 . In the past, Hosha was held on January 15 . “Hosha,” i.e., shooting a {{jalink|bow|Q19827042|bow}} on foot (not on horseback), is a Shinto rite for warding off evil and divining the year’s fortunes . It is connected to a tradition of Azumi Momotari (百足) slaying an earth spider (tsuchigumo) . : In Hosha, young men chosen from parishioners serve as archers and shoot at a large target set up along the approach . Preparations begin on January 2 and proceed through various rituals, forming a traditional rite . It is designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival” . ; Yamahome Tanemaki Gyoryō-sai / Yamahome Gyoryō-sai : Also called the “Yamahome Festival.” The spring Yamahome Tanemaki Gyoryō-sai is held on April 15, and the autumn Yamahome Gyoryō-sai on November 15 . Formerly they were held on lunar February 15 and November 15 and were called the “Hunting and Fishing Festival” . The spring rite includes gestures of sowing to pray for a good harvest, while the autumn rite includes gestures of hauling nets to pray for a bountiful catch. : Next, the three Shika mountains (Katsuyama, Kinugasa-yama, and Mikasa-yama) are purified and praised (yamahome) . Then gestures of shooting a deer (hunting rite) and catching sea bream (fishing rite) are performed . It is designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Yamahome Festival” . : As a {{jalink|kagura song|Q11590393}}, the following song is sung [http://www.sikanosima.jp/event-maturi/yamafome08/index2.html Yamahome Gyoryō Festival] (personal website).. {{Cquote|Kimigayo wa / chiyo ni yachiyo ni / sazareishi no / iwao to narite koke no musu made
Are haya / are koso wa / wagakimi no mifune kaya / utsurōgase migai ni inochi / senzai to iu
Hana koso / saitara / oki no onzu no shiohaya ni haetaram tsuruo ni kuwazaram / tai wa oki no murendai hoya

Shika no hama / nagaki o mireba / ikuyo heranamu / Kashii-ji ni muita ru ano fukiage no hama / chiyo ni yachiyo made
Koyoi yowa ni tsuki tamau / mifune koso / taga mifune arikeru yo / are haya / are koso wa / Azumi no kimi no meshi tamau / mifune ni narikeru yo
Iruka yo / iruka / shiohaya no iruka / Isora ga saki ni / tai tsuru okina|20px||Yamahome Festival Kagura Song}} It closely resembles “{{jalink|Kimigayo|Q81534}},” Japan’s {{jalink|national anthem|Q23691}}, but according to Kinoshita Mishige (father of Kinoshita Norio, former chief priest of {{jalink|Kashii Shrine|Q631373}}), records of Tsukushi kagura once held at Kashii Shrine show that this Yamahome Festival kagura song spread via traveling performers, was included in the *Kokin Wakashū*, later became the “Kimigayo” found in the Satsuma biwa piece “Hōraisan,” and then became the national anthem. It is also said that similar kagura songs are transmitted at Najima Shrine in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, and at {{jalink|Fūromiya|Q11282543}} in {{jalink|Ōkawa City|Q385248}}, {{jalink|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258}} (the priests of the three shrines—Shikaumi, Najima, and Fūromiya—are all of the Azumi lineage). ; Tanabata Festival : A festival held from August 6 to 7 praying for safe fishing and a good catch . Formerly it was held on lunar July 7 [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/123 Tanabata Festival of Shikaumi Shrine] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. : During the festival, fishermen of Hakata Bay visit the port on boats flying big-catch flags, then worship at Shikaumi Shrine . The festival is also mentioned in Kaibara Ekken’s *Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki*, and it is said that in earlier times there were many stalls . ; Otokoyama Festival : A rite held on October 1 to decide by {{jalink|lottery|Q5433694}} whether the year’s grand festival will include a procession . Formerly it was held on lunar September 1 . However, today the procession is conducted biennially . === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Property (national designation) === * Gilded bell (鍍金鐘) (craft) *: A {{jalink|Buddhist bell|Q8192099}} (Korean bell) transmitted at Shikaumi Shrine, retaining traces of gilding (“tokin” meaning plating) on its surface. Though small (height 52.8 cm; mouth diameter 30.5 cm), it is characterized by a relatively large dragon handle at the top. The upper and lower bands bear peony arabesque patterns, and four striking pads with sixteen-petaled lotus designs are placed slightly above the lower band. Four seated Buddha images are cast on the bell body, with two heavenly guardian figures beneath each. The bell is unsigned, but its form resembles the Korean bell at {{jalink|Mandaraji|Q11515245}} in {{jalink|Kōnan, Aichi|Q820496}}, which bears a date corresponding to 1234 CE, and it is thought to date to the early 13th century in the {{jalink|Goryeo|Q28208}} period Ryohei Tsuboi, *Revised: Bonshō and Ancient Culture* (Business Education Publishing, 1993), pp. 302–304.. Deposited at the {{jalink|Fukuoka City Museum|Q11592224}}. Designated April 14, 1906 (Meiji 39). === Fukuoka Prefecture-designated cultural properties === * Tangible cultural properties ** Stone Hōkyōintō pagoda (archaeological material) [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/323 Stone Hōkyōintō Pagoda] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated October 29, 1958 (Shōwa 33). ** Fragmentary mold for a slender bronze sword (archaeological material) **: A casting mold for a {{jalink|slender bronze sword|Q12602346}} estimated to date to the early first half of the Middle Yayoi period; excavated in 1947 from the Katsuma area and owned by Shikaumi Shrine [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/322 Fragmentary Mold for a Slender Bronze Sword] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. The mold is sandstone; both ends are missing, and the remaining length is 18.1 cm . Designated July 26, 1958 (Shōwa 33). * Intangible folk cultural properties ** Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/112 Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated March 31, 1959 (Shōwa 34). ** Yamahome Festival [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/115 Yamahome Festival] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated January 12, 1960 (Shōwa 35). ** Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/133 Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated August 16, 1960 (Shōwa 35). === Fukuoka City-designated cultural properties === * Tangible cultural properties ** Illustrated Shikaumi Shrine origin scrolls, 3 hanging scrolls (painting) — Deposited at Fukuoka City Museum. Designated March 7, 1985 (Shōwa 60). ** Shikaumi Shrine documents, 45 items (books/manuscripts/old texts) — Designated March 7, 1985 (Shōwa 60). * Tangible folk cultural property ** Power stones of Shikaumi Shrine **: Edo-period {{jalink|power stones|Q1660393}} beside the shrine worship hall [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/427 Power Stones of Shikaumi Shrine] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. A natural basalt stone: length 66 cm, width 36 cm, weight 118.2 kg . Designated March 2006 (Heisei 18). === Shrine temple (jingūji) === Shikaumi Shrine formerly had a *jingūji* temple called **Kongōzan Kisshōji** . It is said to have been founded during the {{jalink|Eikyō|Q1193059}} era ({{jalink|1429|Q6326}}–{{jalink|1441|Q6402}}) . Originally {{jalink|Tendai|Q668188}}, it later changed to {{jalink|Zen|Q7953}} and became a branch temple of Hakata’s {{jalink|Shōfukuji|Q3191242}} . The temple grounds included a Monju hall and had flourishing devotion to {{jalink|Manjushri|Q471696|Monju}}, and it is said to have been worshiped as a guardian of seafaring as well . Kisshōji was abolished in March {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 1 ({{jalink|1868|Q7717}}) due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism . It is thought that Sōgonji, located south of Shikaumi Shrine, inherited Kisshōji’s lineage . Sōgonji preserves a Heian-period wooden standing Kannon (Fukuoka City-designated tangible cultural property) and a Nanboku-chō-period bronze seated bodhisattva (also Fukuoka City-designated tangible cultural property). === Works in which it appears === * *{{jalink|Man’yōshū|Q834321}}*, vol. 7, poem no. 1230 *Man’yōshū*, vol. 7, no. 1230 (see [http://infux03.inf.edu.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/~manyou/ver2_2/manyou_kekka3.php?kekka=1232 07/1230] in Yamaguchi University’s “Man’yōshū Search System”). *: {{Cquote|Travel poem
Chihayaburu / Kane no misaki o / suginutomo / ware wa wasureji / Shika no sumerokami
(ちはやぶる かねのみさきを すぎぬとも われはわすれじ しかのすめかみ)|20px||*Man’yōshū* vol. 7, no. 1230}} * Noh play “Watatsumi” ({{jalink|Yōkyoku|Q8062662}} / {{jalink|Noh|Q226887}}) — long discontinued but revived in recent {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} |創建 = Unknown |本殿 = Three-bay nagare-zukuri{{jalink|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684}}{{jalink|Hiwada-buki|Q90373477}} |別名 = |札所等 = |例祭 = Second Monday of October (Kokudo Festival) |神事 = Ayumi-ya Festival (mid-January)

Tanabata Festival ({{jalink|August 6|Q2787}}–{{jalink|August 7|Q2781|7th}})

Yamayotakashi Fishing and Hunting Festival ({{jalink|November 15|Q2982}}) |地図 = {{Location map|Fukuoka city|label=Shikaumi Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|frame-height=200}} }} {{座標一覧}} [[File:Shikaumi-jinja ichinotorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|First torii gate}}]] '''Shikaumi Shrine''' (しかうみじんじゃ) is a {{jalink|Shinto shrine|Q845945}} located in {{jalink|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258}}{{jalink|Fukuoka City|Q26600}}{{jalink|Higashi Ward (Fukuoka City)|Q1206659|Higashi Ward}}{{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}. It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}} ({{jalink|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964}}). Under the {{jalink|modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|former shrine ranking}}, it was classified as a {{jalink|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|Kanpei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} of the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. It claims to be the head shrine of all {{jalink|Watatsumi shrines|Q11607434}} and {{jalink|Kaijin shrines|Q123530063}} nationwide. It is praised as the “capital of dragons” and is known as a place associated with the ancient clan {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}} (also written Adzumi). === Shrine name === Regarding the origin of the word “Shika” (志賀), which is also the island name of {{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}, an excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* Excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* cited in *Shaku Nihongi*, vol. 6, section on the deities worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji, etc. says that, based on a tradition connected to {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s expedition to {{jalink|Silla|Q28456}}, the area was called “Chikashima (近島, ‘near island’),” which later shifted in pronunciation to “Shikashima (資珂島)” . The shrine name “Shikaumi” (志賀海) is now pronounced “Shikaumi,” but as for the original pronunciation there are various theories such as “Shika no Wata,” “Shika no Ama,” “Shika no Umi,” and “Shika ni Imasu Wata,” among others . === Enshrined deities === The deities are enshrined as follows: one principal deity in each of the left, center, and right halls, along with one associated deity in each hall . The three principal deities are collectively called the “{{jalink|Watatsumi|Q1474187|Watatsumi Three Deities}}” (綿津見三神, watatsumi sanshin) . * Left Hall: **Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (仲津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Left Hall: {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}} (神功皇后) * Center Hall: **Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami** (底津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Center Hall: {{jalink|Tamayorihime (Hyūga myth)|Q3082751|Princess Tamayorihime}} (玉依姫命) * Right Hall: **Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (表津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Right Hall: {{jalink|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997}} (応神天皇) === About the enshrined deities === The three Watatsumi (sea / Watatsumi / Watatsumi of the “少童” reading) deities are regarded as sea gods, as seen in the ancient name for the sea “Wata / Watanohara” (“sea = wata, watanohara”) “Kaijin Shinkō” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.. In the “birth of the gods” section of the {{jalink|Kojiki|Q813031}} and {{jalink|Nihon Shoki|Q813935}}, during the purification rite ({{jalink|misogi}}), they are described as gods born together with the {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}} as follows. * *Kojiki* *: It calls the three born deities—Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami, Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami, and Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami—collectively “Watatsumi no Kami,” and states, “They are the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji (あずみのむらじ) and others venerate as their ancestral deity” . * *Nihon Shoki* *: After saying, “The sea gods born were named Sukunahiko no Mikoto,” it records that the three born deities—Sokotsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, Nakatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, and Uwatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto—are “the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji and others worship” . Thus, in the *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*, the Watatsumi Three Deities are treated as the ancestral gods or worshiped gods of the **{{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}}** (Azumi-uji/Azumi-uji; also written 安曇氏, 阿曇族, 安曇族) . The reading “Azumi/Azumi” is also seen as an abbreviation of “Amatsumi (海津見),” and the Azumi clan who served these deities were a *tomonomiyatsuko* clan that oversaw groups of seafaring people “Watatsumi no Kami” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.. In the {{jalink|Sendai Kujihongi|Q2716751}} *Sendai Kujihongi*, “Onmyō Hongi” (see [{{NDLDC|991097/110}} *Kokushi Taikei*, vol. 7] (Keizai Zasshisha, 1897–1901; National Diet Library Digital Collection), frame 110)., likewise in the section on the birth of the gods, it says: “The three Sukunahiko deities are worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji and others; they are the Tsukushi Shika gods,” and Shikaumi Shrine is named as a clan deity under the title “Tsukushi Shika no Kami (筑紫斯香神)” . As other major sea gods besides Watatsumi, Sumiyoshi ({{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}}; worshiped by the Sumiyoshi clan) and Munakata ({{jalink|Munakata Three Goddesses|Q10948069}}; worshiped by the {{jalink|Munakata clan|Q16481907|Munakata lineage}}) are well known, and in northern Kyūshū there are shrines dedicated to each: {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka City)|Q29682|Sumiyoshi Shrine}} and {{jalink|Munakata Taisha|Q704962}}. === History === [[File:Shikanoshima Island, enkei.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}, where Shikaumi Shrine is located}}]] === Founding === The founding date is unknown . According to shrine tradition, in ancient times it consisted of three shrines on Katsuma Beach on the north side of {{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}: Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū; but {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974}} (Azumi no Isora: ancestor of the {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}}) relocated the Uwatsu-gū to the south side of Shikanoshima, making it the present precinct . Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines . Azumi no Isora is also said to have served as helmsman in {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s expedition to {{jalink|Silla|Q28456}} . In ancient northern Kyūshū, the {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}} (also written 安曇氏), who governed sea people ({{jalink|ama|Q1577970}}), are said to have controlled maritime routes . Shikanoshima was a key point for sea traffic, and the area including Shikanoshima and {{jalink|Umi no Nakamichi|Q2404998}} Considered the area of Shika-gō and Azumi-gō in Kasuya District of Chikuzen Province as seen in the *Wamyōshō* (from the *Dictionary of Personal Names of Ancient Japanese Clans*, entry on the Azumi clan). Shika-gō is identified with Shikanoshima; Azumi-gō is identified with the area from Kamiwajiro and Shimowajiro in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City to Shingū Town in Kasuya District, or with Shikanoshima (from *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entries on Shika-gō and Azumi-gō). is said to have been the Azumi clan’s home base *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine., and Shikaumi Shrine is thought to have been the clan’s central shrine . Even today, all of Shikanoshima is regarded as a sacred precinct *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikanoshima., and the current priestly family also claims descent from the Azumi clan . The Azumi clan is said to have expanded throughout Japan, and place names such as “Shika” and “Atsumi”—for example {{jalink|Azumino City|Q534667}} in {{jalink|Nagano Prefecture|Q127877}}, {{jalink|Shika Town|Q1349406}} in {{jalink|Hakuigun|Q1130953}} of {{jalink|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281}}, the {{jalink|Adogawa|Q11450763}} in {{jalink|Shiga Prefecture|Q131358}}, and the {{jalink|Atsumi Peninsula|Q757798}} in {{jalink|Aichi Prefecture|Q80434}}—are said to be toponymic traces of their presence . Shikanoshima is also known for the discovery of the gold seal ({{jalink|King of Na of Wa gold seal|Q2975212}}), but it is unclear why the seal of {{jalink|Na|Q600473}} was found there. Some theories speculate a connection between the Azumi clan—and by extension Shikaumi Shrine as their clan deity—and Na, and at Najima Shrine in Najima, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, the Azumi clan is regarded as the “Nake-nushi” {{Cite web|和書|url=https://lunabura.exblog.jp/14132415/|title=Najima Shrine|accessdate=April 13, 2010|publisher=Ayasugi Luna}}. === Overview history === In surviving records, there is mention in the “Sumiyoshi Taisha Shige (Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki)”—dated Tenpyō 3 ({{jalink|731|Q23566}}), though likely compiled around the early {{jalink|Heian period|Q193292}}—of “Naka District Azumi Shrine, three offerings” and “Shika Shrine” . Also, in the {{jalink|Shinshō Kakuchokufushō|Q11502312}} *Shinshō Kakuchokufushō* 10, “Shinji Shoke Fuko,” directive of Daidō 1 (806) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}})., it appears that as of {{jalink|Daidō (era)|Q1373191|Daidō}} 1 ({{jalink|806|Q30021}}), “Azumi no Kami” had eight households as *shinpu* (donated *fuko*) . According to national histories, in {{jalink|Ten’an|Q1075611|Ten’an}} 3 ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}) the divine rank (*shinkai*) of “Shikaumi no Kami” was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, and in {{jalink|Gangyō|Q747451}} 4 ({{jalink|880|Q23618}}) “Katsuma no Kami” (identified with Nakatsu-gū) was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade . In the “Register of Deities” (*Jinmyōchō*) of the {{jalink|Engishiki|Q1342448}} compiled in {{jalink|Enchō|Q1327274|Enchō}} 5 ({{jalink|927|Q30470}}), it is listed under Naka District of {{jalink|Chikuzen Province|Q1047664}} as “Shikaumi Shrine, three seats, all Myōjin Taisha,” and is ranked as a {{jalink|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964}} . Other Heian and Kamakura-period sources concerning Shikaumi Shrine are few ; in the {{jalink|Shōyūki|Q11459316}} *Shōyūki*, entries for August 27 and August 30, Manju 4 (1027)., there is a note that in {{jalink|Manju|Q1194155}} 3 ({{jalink|1026|Q19269}}) the shrine’s priest traveled to {{jalink|Song dynasty|Q7462}} (entered Song) and returned the following year . [[File:Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba e20(2).JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Torii and shrine buildings depicted in the {{jalink|Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba|Q3087790}}}}]] In the {{jalink|Kamakura period|Q236205}}, during the {{jalink|Mongol invasions of Japan|Q208156}}, Shikanoshima became a battlefield, but Shikaumi Shrine’s precinct is recorded in the *Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba* under the name “Shikanoshima Daimyōjin” . From the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012}} onward, Shikaumi Shrine came strongly under warrior control . In {{jalink|Ōnin|Q1143903}} 3 ({{jalink|1469|Q6566}}), Shōni Yoritada confirmed the office of Shikanoshima’s chief priest for the abbot of Tōgetsuji on Tsushima , and afterward it received patronage from the {{jalink|Ōuchi clan|Q1348909}} . It is also said that before sailing to {{jalink|Ming|Q9903}}, people prayed here for safe voyages . In the early modern era, it received protection from the {{jalink|Kobayakawa clan|Q2975298}} and {{jalink|Kuroda clan|Q2975305}} who ruled Chikuzen Province . It is said that {{jalink|Kuroda Nagamasa|Q950496}}, who entered the province in {{jalink|Keichō|Q1328185}} 5 ({{jalink|1600|Q6720}}), built the main sanctuary, worship hall, rōmon gate, and other structures . In {{jalink|Bunka era|Q1373146|Bunka}} 14 ({{jalink|1817|Q6958}}), the shrine lands amounted to 50 koku . In {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 5 ({{jalink|1872|Q7753}}), under the modern shrine ranking system, it was designated a village shrine, and in {{jalink|Taishō|Q329174}} 15 ({{jalink|1926|Q5259}}) it was promoted to *Kanpei Shōsha* “Shikaumi Shrine” entry, *Nihon no Kamigami*.. === Divine ranks === * {{jalink|Ten’an|Q1075611|Ten’an}} 3 ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}) January 27: Shikaumi no Kami from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for January 27, Jōgan 1 (859) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}}). * {{jalink|Gangyō|Q747451}} 4 ({{jalink|880|Q23618}}) March 22: Katsuma no Kami from Senior Sixth Rank, Upper Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for March 22, Gangyō 4 (880). — From the divine name “Katsuma (賀津万),” identified with the subordinate shrine Nakatsu-gū (Katsuma Myōjin) *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine.. === Precincts === [[File:Shikaumi-jinja shaden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Worship hall (front) and main sanctuary (rear right)}}]] The precinct is located on the south side of Shikanoshima. It is said that Shikaumi Shrine was formerly on the north side of Shikanoshima and consisted of three shrines—Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū . Of these, Uwatsu-gū was transferred here and became the present main shrine, while Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines. The former site of Uwatsu-gū is said to be in Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|13.00|N|130|17|32.74|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Site of Uwatsu-gū (former location)}}). In the precinct’s Rokkakudō (鹿角堂), many deer antlers—said to number over ten thousand—have been dedicated. There is also a sacred stone dedicated in later times called the “Kameishi (亀石, ‘turtle stone’),” linked to a tradition that during {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s {{jalink|Three Kingdoms expedition|Q11249435}}, {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974}} appeared before the empress riding a turtle . Along the approach stands a stone *Hōkyōintō* pagoda. A {{jalink|Hōkyōintō|Q3146365}} is a pagoda that enshrines a Buddhist scripture (the *Hōkyōin Dharani Sutra*) Explanatory signboard in the precinct.. This one bears an inscription from {{jalink|Jōwa|Q1146143|Jōwa}} 3 ({{jalink|1347|Q6082}}) in the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012}}, and is the oldest complete example in Fukuoka Prefecture . Made of {{jalink|granite|Q41177}}, it consists of a base, body, roof, and finial, with a total height of 334.5 cm . It is designated a tangible cultural property of Fukuoka Prefecture . The first torii was built in {{jalink|Kanbun|Q1146228}} 10 ({{jalink|1670|Q7606}}) by {{jalink|Kuroda Mitsuyuki|Q11678571}}, the third lord of the {{jalink|Fukuoka Domain|Q208766}} . The next torii was built in {{jalink|Genroku|Q1325001}} 13 ({{jalink|1700|Q6813}}), and the torii by the seashore was built in An’ei 3 ({{jalink|1774|Q7697}}) . File:Rokkakudō.JPG|Rokkakudō (Deer Antler Hall) File:Shikaumi-jinja kameishi.JPG|Kameishi (Turtle Stone) File:Shikaumi-jinja romon.JPG|Rōmon gate and stone bridge File:Shikaumi-jinja tou.JPG|Hōkyōintō pagoda (Fukuoka Prefecture-designated tangible cultural property) File:Shikaumi-jinja ninotorii.JPG|Second torii === Auxiliary shrines (sessha and massha) === There are a total of 24 auxiliary shrines: 5 sessha and 19 massha Shrine origin pamphlet. . According to the *Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki*, there were once 375 massha, but they were damaged in the Warring States turmoil; at the time of restoration by {{jalink|Ōuchi Mochiyo|Q11432525}} in {{jalink|Eikyō|Q1193059}} 11 ({{jalink|1439|Q6380}}), there were a little over 120, and later in the Edo period there were only about five . === Sessha === [[File:Okitsujima Island near Shikanoshima Island 5.jpg|thumb|200px|{{center|{{jalink|Okitsushima|Q49665728}}, where Okitsu-gū is enshrined}}]] [[File:Torii of Katsuma Shrine (Nakatsu Shrine of Shikaumi Shrine).jpg|thumb|200px|{{center|Torii of Nakatsu-gū}}]] [[File:Shikaumi-jinja Imamiya-jinja.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Imamiya Shrine}}]] * Okitsu-gū (沖津宮) ** Location: Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|20.12|N|130|17|25.07|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Okitsu-gū}}) ** Enshrined deities: Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami, {{jalink|Ame no Minakanushi|Q2842779|Ame no Minakanushi no Kami}} * Nakatsu-gū (仲津宮 / 中津宮) ** Location: Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|11.80|N|130|17|27.45|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Nakatsu-gū}}) ** Enshrined deity: Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami *: Also called “Katsuma Myōjin,” and identified with “Katsuma no Kami” in the {{jalink|Kokushi genzaisha|Q118304363}} . *: In {{jalink|Heisei|Q234510}} 6 ({{jalink|1994|Q2067}}), a kofun (Nakatsu-gū Kofun) was discovered in the forecourt area [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/481 Nakatsu-gū Kofun] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. Because it was damaged by shrine construction, its size and form are unclear, but grave goods were found along with a pit-type stone chamber . It is dated to the first half of the {{jalink|7th century|Q8089}} and is regarded as the tomb of a leader of the local maritime group . * Imamiya Shrine (今宮神社) ** Location: within the main shrine precinct ({{Coord|33|40|4.89|N|130|18|46.38|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Imamiya Shrine}}) ** Enshrined deities: {{jalink|Utsushi Hikane no Mikoto|Q86736058}}, {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}}, {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974|Azumi no Isora-maru}}, and other ancestral Azumi deities * Hiroten Shrine (弘天神社) ** Location: Hiro, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|40|15.19|N|130|17|34.32|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Hiroten Shrine}}) ** Enshrined deities: {{jalink|Izanagi|Q813858|Izanagi no Mikoto}}, {{jalink|Izanami|Q682306|Izanami no Mikoto}} * Ōtake Shrine (大嶽神社) ** Location: Ōtake, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|39|23.19|N|130|20|8.05|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Sessha: Ōtake Shrine}}) ** Enshrined deities: {{jalink|Shinatsuhiko|Q1073925|Shinatsuhiko no Kami}}, Shinatsuhime no Kami, Ōhama Sukune, {{jalink|Uke-mochi|Q2280323}} === Massha === There are 19 massha in total: 12 in Shika, 5 in Katsuma, 1 in Hiro, and 1 in Ōtake . File:Shikaumi-jinja massha.JPG|Group of massha within the precinct File:Shikaumi-jinja Innyaku-sha.JPG|Innyaku Shrine === Festivals === === Annual grand festival === Shikaumi Shrine’s annual grand festival is called the “Kunchi Festival” (国土祭). On the previous day, every other year (odd-numbered years in the Western calendar), the shrine’s largest festival, the “Goshinkō Festival” (御神幸祭), is held . In the past it was held on the old lunar calendar: September 8 (Goshinkō Festival) and September 9 (Kunchi Festival), but today it is held on {{jalink|Health and Sports Day}} and the day before (the second Monday of October and the preceding day) . Before the festival, on lunar September 1 (October 1), a “Otokoyama Festival” is held in which a {{jalink|lottery|Q5433694}} determines whether to conduct the procession (today it is held biennially) . In the Goshinkō Festival, beginning at 9 p.m. on the night of lunar September 8 (the night before Health and Sports Day), three mikoshi (Ichinoto, Ninoto, Sannotō) depart and proceed to a temporary shrine (tonomiya) . There, performances based on the shrine’s origin traditions—such as the “Dragon Dance,” “Yaotome Dance,” and “Kakko Dance”—are dedicated . The mikoshi then return to the shrine, the spirit is transferred back to the main sanctuary, and the Goshinkō Festival ends . On the following day, lunar September 9 (Health and Sports Day), *yabusame* ({{jalink|horseback archery|Q1886157}}) is offered . Because it involves moving the divine spirit at night and aims to reaffirm the tradition for the people through performances rooted in the shrine’s origin narrative, the Goshinkō Festival is said to preserve an ancient form . The rites are designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event” . === Special rites === ; Hosha Festival : “Hosha-sai.” A New Year rite held among annual events from January 2 to 15, conducted on a Sunday near January 15 . In the past, Hosha was held on January 15 . “Hosha,” i.e., shooting a {{jalink|bow|Q19827042|bow}} on foot (not on horseback), is a Shinto rite for warding off evil and divining the year’s fortunes . It is connected to a tradition of Azumi Momotari (百足) slaying an earth spider (tsuchigumo) . : In Hosha, young men chosen from parishioners serve as archers and shoot at a large target set up along the approach . Preparations begin on January 2 and proceed through various rituals, forming a traditional rite . It is designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival” . ; Yamahome Tanemaki Gyoryō-sai / Yamahome Gyoryō-sai : Also called the “Yamahome Festival.” The spring Yamahome Tanemaki Gyoryō-sai is held on April 15, and the autumn Yamahome Gyoryō-sai on November 15 . Formerly they were held on lunar February 15 and November 15 and were called the “Hunting and Fishing Festival” . The spring rite includes gestures of sowing to pray for a good harvest, while the autumn rite includes gestures of hauling nets to pray for a bountiful catch. : Next, the three Shika mountains (Katsuyama, Kinugasa-yama, and Mikasa-yama) are purified and praised (yamahome) . Then gestures of shooting a deer (hunting rite) and catching sea bream (fishing rite) are performed . It is designated a Fukuoka Prefecture intangible folk cultural property as the “Yamahome Festival” . : As a {{jalink|kagura song|Q11590393}}, the following song is sung [http://www.sikanosima.jp/event-maturi/yamafome08/index2.html Yamahome Gyoryō Festival] (personal website).. {{Cquote|Kimigayo wa / chiyo ni yachiyo ni / sazareishi no / iwao to narite koke no musu made
Are haya / are koso wa / wagakimi no mifune kaya / utsurōgase migai ni inochi / senzai to iu
Hana koso / saitara / oki no onzu no shiohaya ni haetaram tsuruo ni kuwazaram / tai wa oki no murendai hoya

Shika no hama / nagaki o mireba / ikuyo heranamu / Kashii-ji ni muita ru ano fukiage no hama / chiyo ni yachiyo made
Koyoi yowa ni tsuki tamau / mifune koso / taga mifune arikeru yo / are haya / are koso wa / Azumi no kimi no meshi tamau / mifune ni narikeru yo
Iruka yo / iruka / shiohaya no iruka / Isora ga saki ni / tai tsuru okina|20px||Yamahome Festival Kagura Song}} It closely resembles “{{jalink|Kimigayo|Q81534}},” Japan’s {{jalink|national anthem|Q23691}}, but according to Kinoshita Mishige (father of Kinoshita Norio, former chief priest of {{jalink|Kashii Shrine|Q631373}}), records of Tsukushi kagura once held at Kashii Shrine show that this Yamahome Festival kagura song spread via traveling performers, was included in the *Kokin Wakashū*, later became the “Kimigayo” found in the Satsuma biwa piece “Hōraisan,” and then became the national anthem. It is also said that similar kagura songs are transmitted at Najima Shrine in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, and at {{jalink|Fūromiya|Q11282543}} in {{jalink|Ōkawa City|Q385248}}, {{jalink|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258}} (the priests of the three shrines—Shikaumi, Najima, and Fūromiya—are all of the Azumi lineage). ; Tanabata Festival : A festival held from August 6 to 7 praying for safe fishing and a good catch . Formerly it was held on lunar July 7 [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/123 Tanabata Festival of Shikaumi Shrine] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. : During the festival, fishermen of Hakata Bay visit the port on boats flying big-catch flags, then worship at Shikaumi Shrine . The festival is also mentioned in Kaibara Ekken’s *Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki*, and it is said that in earlier times there were many stalls . ; Otokoyama Festival : A rite held on October 1 to decide by {{jalink|lottery|Q5433694}} whether the year’s grand festival will include a procession . Formerly it was held on lunar September 1 . However, today the procession is conducted biennially . === Cultural properties === === Important Cultural Property (national designation) === * Gilded bell (鍍金鐘) (craft) *: A {{jalink|Buddhist bell|Q8192099}} (Korean bell) transmitted at Shikaumi Shrine, retaining traces of gilding (“tokin” meaning plating) on its surface. Though small (height 52.8 cm; mouth diameter 30.5 cm), it is characterized by a relatively large dragon handle at the top. The upper and lower bands bear peony arabesque patterns, and four striking pads with sixteen-petaled lotus designs are placed slightly above the lower band. Four seated Buddha images are cast on the bell body, with two heavenly guardian figures beneath each. The bell is unsigned, but its form resembles the Korean bell at {{jalink|Mandaraji|Q11515245}} in {{jalink|Kōnan, Aichi|Q820496}}, which bears a date corresponding to 1234 CE, and it is thought to date to the early 13th century in the {{jalink|Goryeo|Q28208}} period Ryohei Tsuboi, *Revised: Bonshō and Ancient Culture* (Business Education Publishing, 1993), pp. 302–304.. Deposited at the {{jalink|Fukuoka City Museum|Q11592224}}. Designated April 14, 1906 (Meiji 39). === Fukuoka Prefecture-designated cultural properties === * Tangible cultural properties ** Stone Hōkyōintō pagoda (archaeological material) [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/323 Stone Hōkyōintō Pagoda] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated October 29, 1958 (Shōwa 33). ** Fragmentary mold for a slender bronze sword (archaeological material) **: A casting mold for a {{jalink|slender bronze sword|Q12602346}} estimated to date to the early first half of the Middle Yayoi period; excavated in 1947 from the Katsuma area and owned by Shikaumi Shrine [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/322 Fragmentary Mold for a Slender Bronze Sword] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. The mold is sandstone; both ends are missing, and the remaining length is 18.1 cm . Designated July 26, 1958 (Shōwa 33). * Intangible folk cultural properties ** Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/112 Shikaumi Shrine Hosha Festival] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated March 31, 1959 (Shōwa 34). ** Yamahome Festival [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/115 Yamahome Festival] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated January 12, 1960 (Shōwa 35). ** Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/133 Shikaumi Shrine Shinkō Event] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”). — Designated August 16, 1960 (Shōwa 35). === Fukuoka City-designated cultural properties === * Tangible cultural properties ** Illustrated Shikaumi Shrine origin scrolls, 3 hanging scrolls (painting) — Deposited at Fukuoka City Museum. Designated March 7, 1985 (Shōwa 60). ** Shikaumi Shrine documents, 45 items (books/manuscripts/old texts) — Designated March 7, 1985 (Shōwa 60). * Tangible folk cultural property ** Power stones of Shikaumi Shrine **: Edo-period {{jalink|power stones|Q1660393}} beside the shrine worship hall [http://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/427 Power Stones of Shikaumi Shrine] (Fukuoka City Economic Tourism and Culture Bureau, “Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City”).. A natural basalt stone: length 66 cm, width 36 cm, weight 118.2 kg . Designated March 2006 (Heisei 18). === Shrine temple (jingūji) === Shikaumi Shrine formerly had a *jingūji* temple called **Kongōzan Kisshōji** . It is said to have been founded during the {{jalink|Eikyō|Q1193059}} era ({{jalink|1429|Q6326}}–{{jalink|1441|Q6402}}) . Originally {{jalink|Tendai|Q668188}}, it later changed to {{jalink|Zen|Q7953}} and became a branch temple of Hakata’s {{jalink|Shōfukuji|Q3191242}} . The temple grounds included a Monju hall and had flourishing devotion to {{jalink|Manjushri|Q471696|Monju}}, and it is said to have been worshiped as a guardian of seafaring as well . Kisshōji was abolished in March {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 1 ({{jalink|1868|Q7717}}) due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism . It is thought that Sōgonji, located south of Shikaumi Shrine, inherited Kisshōji’s lineage . Yamayotakashi Fishing and Hunting Festival ({{jalink|November 15|Q2982}}) |地図 = {{Location map|Fukuoka city|label=Shikaumi Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|frame-height=200}} }} {{座標一覧}} [[File:Shikaumi-jinja ichinotorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|First torii gate}}]] '''Shikaumi Shrine''' (しかうみじんじゃ) is a {{jalink|Shinto shrine|Q845945}} located in {{jalink|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258}}{{jalink|Fukuoka City|Q26600}}{{jalink|Higashi Ward (Fukuoka City)|Q1206659|Higashi Ward}}{{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}. It is a {{jalink|Shikinaisha}} ({{jalink|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964}}). Under the {{jalink|modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|former shrine ranking}}, it was classified as a {{jalink|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines#Government shrines|Q712534|Kanpei-shōsha}}, and today it is a {{jalink|Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274}} of the {{jalink|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077}}. It claims to be the head shrine of all {{jalink|Watatsumi shrines|Q11607434}} and {{jalink|Kaijin shrines|Q123530063}} nationwide. It is praised as the “capital of dragons” and is known as a place associated with the ancient clan {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}} (also written Adzumi). === Shrine name === Regarding the origin of the word “Shika” (志賀), which is also the island name of {{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}, an excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* Excerpt from the *Chikuzen no Kuni Fudoki* cited in *Shaku Nihongi*, vol. 6, section on the deities worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji, etc. says that, based on a tradition connected to {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s expedition to {{jalink|Silla|Q28456}}, the area was called “Chikashima (近島, ‘near island’),” which later shifted in pronunciation to “Shikashima (資珂島)” . The shrine name “Shikaumi” (志賀海) is now pronounced “Shikaumi,” but as for the original pronunciation there are various theories such as “Shika no Wata,” “Shika no Ama,” “Shika no Umi,” and “Shika ni Imasu Wata,” among others . === Enshrined deities === The deities are enshrined as follows: one principal deity in each of the left, center, and right halls, along with one associated deity in each hall . The three principal deities are collectively called the “{{jalink|Watatsumi|Q1474187|Watatsumi Three Deities}}” (綿津見三神, watatsumi sanshin) . * Left Hall: **Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (仲津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Left Hall: {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}} (神功皇后) * Center Hall: **Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami** (底津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Center Hall: {{jalink|Tamayorihime (Hyūga myth)|Q3082751|Princess Tamayorihime}} (玉依姫命) * Right Hall: **Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami** (表津綿津見神) ** Associated deity of the Right Hall: {{jalink|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997}} (応神天皇) === About the enshrined deities === The three Watatsumi (sea / Watatsumi / Watatsumi of the “少童” reading) deities are regarded as sea gods, as seen in the ancient name for the sea “Wata / Watanohara” (“sea = wata, watanohara”) “Kaijin Shinkō” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.. In the “birth of the gods” section of the {{jalink|Kojiki|Q813031}} and {{jalink|Nihon Shoki|Q813935}}, during the purification rite ({{jalink|misogi}}), they are described as gods born together with the {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}} as follows. * *Kojiki* *: It calls the three born deities—Sokotsu Watatsumi no Kami, Nakatsu Watatsumi no Kami, and Uwatsu Watatsumi no Kami—collectively “Watatsumi no Kami,” and states, “They are the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji (あずみのむらじ) and others venerate as their ancestral deity” . * *Nihon Shoki* *: After saying, “The sea gods born were named Sukunahiko no Mikoto,” it records that the three born deities—Sokotsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, Nakatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto, and Uwatsu Sukunahiko no Mikoto—are “the gods whom the Azumi no Muraji and others worship” . Thus, in the *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*, the Watatsumi Three Deities are treated as the ancestral gods or worshiped gods of the **{{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}}** (Azumi-uji/Azumi-uji; also written 安曇氏, 阿曇族, 安曇族) . The reading “Azumi/Azumi” is also seen as an abbreviation of “Amatsumi (海津見),” and the Azumi clan who served these deities were a *tomonomiyatsuko* clan that oversaw groups of seafaring people “Watatsumi no Kami” entry, *Kokushi Daijiten*.. In the {{jalink|Sendai Kujihongi|Q2716751}} *Sendai Kujihongi*, “Onmyō Hongi” (see [{{NDLDC|991097/110}} *Kokushi Taikei*, vol. 7] (Keizai Zasshisha, 1897–1901; National Diet Library Digital Collection), frame 110)., likewise in the section on the birth of the gods, it says: “The three Sukunahiko deities are worshiped by the Azumi no Muraji and others; they are the Tsukushi Shika gods,” and Shikaumi Shrine is named as a clan deity under the title “Tsukushi Shika no Kami (筑紫斯香神)” . As other major sea gods besides Watatsumi, Sumiyoshi ({{jalink|Sumiyoshi Three Deities|Q1114013}}; worshiped by the Sumiyoshi clan) and Munakata ({{jalink|Munakata Three Goddesses|Q10948069}}; worshiped by the {{jalink|Munakata clan|Q16481907|Munakata lineage}}) are well known, and in northern Kyūshū there are shrines dedicated to each: {{jalink|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka City)|Q29682|Sumiyoshi Shrine}} and {{jalink|Munakata Taisha|Q704962}}. === History === [[File:Shikanoshima Island, enkei.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}, where Shikaumi Shrine is located}}]] === Founding === The founding date is unknown . According to shrine tradition, in ancient times it consisted of three shrines on Katsuma Beach on the north side of {{jalink|Shikanoshima|Q3077260}}: Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū; but {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974}} (Azumi no Isora: ancestor of the {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}}) relocated the Uwatsu-gū to the south side of Shikanoshima, making it the present precinct . Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines . Azumi no Isora is also said to have served as helmsman in {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s expedition to {{jalink|Silla|Q28456}} . In ancient northern Kyūshū, the {{jalink|Azumi clan|Q3377806}} (also written 安曇氏), who governed sea people ({{jalink|ama|Q1577970}}), are said to have controlled maritime routes . Shikanoshima was a key point for sea traffic, and the area including Shikanoshima and {{jalink|Umi no Nakamichi|Q2404998}} Considered the area of Shika-gō and Azumi-gō in Kasuya District of Chikuzen Province as seen in the *Wamyōshō* (from the *Dictionary of Personal Names of Ancient Japanese Clans*, entry on the Azumi clan). Shika-gō is identified with Shikanoshima; Azumi-gō is identified with the area from Kamiwajiro and Shimowajiro in Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City to Shingū Town in Kasuya District, or with Shikanoshima (from *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entries on Shika-gō and Azumi-gō). is said to have been the Azumi clan’s home base *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine., and Shikaumi Shrine is thought to have been the clan’s central shrine . Even today, all of Shikanoshima is regarded as a sacred precinct *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten*, entry on Shikanoshima., and the current priestly family also claims descent from the Azumi clan . The Azumi clan is said to have expanded throughout Japan, and place names such as “Shika” and “Atsumi”—for example {{jalink|Azumino City|Q534667}} in {{jalink|Nagano Prefecture|Q127877}}, {{jalink|Shika Town|Q1349406}} in {{jalink|Hakuigun|Q1130953}} of {{jalink|Ishikawa Prefecture|Q131281}}, the {{jalink|Adogawa|Q11450763}} in {{jalink|Shiga Prefecture|Q131358}}, and the {{jalink|Atsumi Peninsula|Q757798}} in {{jalink|Aichi Prefecture|Q80434}}—are said to be toponymic traces of their presence . Shikanoshima is also known for the discovery of the gold seal ({{jalink|King of Na of Wa gold seal|Q2975212}}), but it is unclear why the seal of {{jalink|Na|Q600473}} was found there. Some theories speculate a connection between the Azumi clan—and by extension Shikaumi Shrine as their clan deity—and Na, and at Najima Shrine in Najima, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City, the Azumi clan is regarded as the “Nake-nushi” {{Cite web|和書|url=https://lunabura.exblog.jp/14132415/|title=Najima Shrine|accessdate=April 13, 2010|publisher=Ayasugi Luna}}. === Overview history === In surviving records, there is mention in the “Sumiyoshi Taisha Shige (Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki)”—dated Tenpyō 3 ({{jalink|731|Q23566}}), though likely compiled around the early {{jalink|Heian period|Q193292}}—of “Naka District Azumi Shrine, three offerings” and “Shika Shrine” . Also, in the {{jalink|Shinshō Kakuchokufushō|Q11502312}} *Shinshō Kakuchokufushō* 10, “Shinji Shoke Fuko,” directive of Daidō 1 (806) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}})., it appears that as of {{jalink|Daidō (era)|Q1373191|Daidō}} 1 ({{jalink|806|Q30021}}), “Azumi no Kami” had eight households as *shinpu* (donated *fuko*) . According to national histories, in {{jalink|Ten’an|Q1075611|Ten’an}} 3 ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}) the divine rank (*shinkai*) of “Shikaumi no Kami” was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade, and in {{jalink|Gangyō|Q747451}} 4 ({{jalink|880|Q23618}}) “Katsuma no Kami” (identified with Nakatsu-gū) was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade . In the “Register of Deities” (*Jinmyōchō*) of the {{jalink|Engishiki|Q1342448}} compiled in {{jalink|Enchō|Q1327274|Enchō}} 5 ({{jalink|927|Q30470}}), it is listed under Naka District of {{jalink|Chikuzen Province|Q1047664}} as “Shikaumi Shrine, three seats, all Myōjin Taisha,” and is ranked as a {{jalink|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964}} . Other Heian and Kamakura-period sources concerning Shikaumi Shrine are few ; in the {{jalink|Shōyūki|Q11459316}} *Shōyūki*, entries for August 27 and August 30, Manju 4 (1027)., there is a note that in {{jalink|Manju|Q1194155}} 3 ({{jalink|1026|Q19269}}) the shrine’s priest traveled to {{jalink|Song dynasty|Q7462}} (entered Song) and returned the following year . [[File:Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba e20(2).JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Torii and shrine buildings depicted in the {{jalink|Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba|Q3087790}}}}]] In the {{jalink|Kamakura period|Q236205}}, during the {{jalink|Mongol invasions of Japan|Q208156}}, Shikanoshima became a battlefield, but Shikaumi Shrine’s precinct is recorded in the *Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba* under the name “Shikanoshima Daimyōjin” . From the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012}} onward, Shikaumi Shrine came strongly under warrior control . In {{jalink|Ōnin|Q1143903}} 3 ({{jalink|1469|Q6566}}), Shōni Yoritada confirmed the office of Shikanoshima’s chief priest for the abbot of Tōgetsuji on Tsushima , and afterward it received patronage from the {{jalink|Ōuchi clan|Q1348909}} . It is also said that before sailing to {{jalink|Ming|Q9903}}, people prayed here for safe voyages . In the early modern era, it received protection from the {{jalink|Kobayakawa clan|Q2975298}} and {{jalink|Kuroda clan|Q2975305}} who ruled Chikuzen Province . It is said that {{jalink|Kuroda Nagamasa|Q950496}}, who entered the province in {{jalink|Keichō|Q1328185}} 5 ({{jalink|1600|Q6720}}), built the main sanctuary, worship hall, rōmon gate, and other structures . In {{jalink|Bunka era|Q1373146|Bunka}} 14 ({{jalink|1817|Q6958}}), the shrine lands amounted to 50 koku . In {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} 5 ({{jalink|1872|Q7753}}), under the modern shrine ranking system, it was designated a village shrine, and in {{jalink|Taishō|Q329174}} 15 ({{jalink|1926|Q5259}}) it was promoted to *Kanpei Shōsha* “Shikaumi Shrine” entry, *Nihon no Kamigami*.. === Divine ranks === * {{jalink|Ten’an|Q1075611|Ten’an}} 3 ({{jalink|859|Q23897}}) January 27: Shikaumi no Kami from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for January 27, Jōgan 1 (859) (see {{Harvnb|Shintō / Shrine Historical Sources Compilation}}). * {{jalink|Gangyō|Q747451}} 4 ({{jalink|880|Q23618}}) March 22: Katsuma no Kami from Senior Sixth Rank, Upper Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade (*Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*) *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku*, entry for March 22, Gangyō 4 (880). — From the divine name “Katsuma (賀津万),” identified with the subordinate shrine Nakatsu-gū (Katsuma Myōjin) *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entry on Shikaumi Shrine.. === Precincts === [[File:Shikaumi-jinja shaden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Worship hall (front) and main sanctuary (rear right)}}]] The precinct is located on the south side of Shikanoshima. It is said that Shikaumi Shrine was formerly on the north side of Shikanoshima and consisted of three shrines—Uwatsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū, and Okitsu-gū . Of these, Uwatsu-gū was transferred here and became the present main shrine, while Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū are now subordinate shrines. The former site of Uwatsu-gū is said to be in Katsuma, Higashi Ward, Fukuoka City ({{Coord|33|41|13.00|N|130|17|32.74|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Site of Uwatsu-gū (former location)}}). In the precinct’s Rokkakudō (鹿角堂), many deer antlers—said to number over ten thousand—have been dedicated. There is also a sacred stone dedicated in later times called the “Kameishi (亀石, ‘turtle stone’),” linked to a tradition that during {{jalink|Empress Jingū|Q232803}}’s {{jalink|Three Kingdoms expedition|Q11249435}}, {{jalink|Azumi no Isora|Q1755974}} appeared before the empress riding a turtle . Along the approach stands a stone *Hōkyōintō* pagoda. A {{jalink|Hōkyōintō|Q3146365}} is a pagoda that enshrines a Buddhist scripture (the *Hōkyōin Dharani Sutra*) Explanatory signboard in the precinct.. This one bears an inscription from {{jalink|Jōwa|Q1146143|Jōwa}} 3 ({{jalink|1347|Q6082}}) in the {{jalink|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012}}, and is the oldest complete example in Fukuoka Prefecture . Made of {{jalink|granite|Q41177}}, it consists of a base, body, roof, and finial, with a total height of 334.5 cm . It is designated a tangible cultural property of Fukuoka Prefecture . The first torii was built in {{jalink|Kanbun|Q1146228}} 10 ({{jalink|1670|Q7606}}) by {{jalink|Kuroda Mitsuyuki|Q11678571}}, the third lord of the {{jalink|Fukuoka Domain|Q208766}} . The next torii was built in {{jalink|Genroku|Q1325001}} 13 ({{jalink|1700|Q6813}}), and the torii by the seashore was built in An’ei 3 ({{jalink|1774|Q7697}}) .
